1	# Decisions
2	
3	Durable decisions for this project, with the reasoning. Each exists because the
4	"obvious" alternative looks correct and would be wrong. Read before changing any
5	of them.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 1. Pin `mcp` to 1.28.x. Do not upgrade to 2.x yet.
10	
11	**Decided 2026-07-29.**
12	
13	`mcp[cli]>=1.28.1,<1.29`
14	
15	MCP Python SDK **2.0.0 exists** (released 2026-07-28) and `FOSSA_MCP_IMPLEMENTATION_SCOPE.md`
16	§4.2/§5 instruct using it. We are deliberately not, because this server is published to Docker Hub
17	for external businesses to depend on, and 2.0.0 has no patch releases yet.
18	
19	1.28.1 (released 2026-06-26) is the last 1.x with meaningful soak time. Note 1.29.0 shipped the
20	same day as 2.0.0 — also too new.
21	
22	**Consequences:** `mcp.server.fastmcp.FastMCP` is the correct API for this build, not `MCPServer`.
23	Scanners will flag the pin as behind 2.x. That is expected — do not auto-bump, and do not let a
24	dependency bot do it.
25	
26	**Revisit when** 2.0.x has patch releases and real-world use. The migration is mechanical but not
27	trivial: 2.0.0 renames `fastmcp` → `mcpserver` and `FastMCP` → `MCPServer`, moves model fields to
28	snake_case (`read_only_hint`, `input_schema`), and relocates `Context` to
29	`mcp.server.mcpserver.context`. Keep the tool layer thin so the swap stays cheap.
30	
31	---
32	
33	## 2. Single-tenant only. Do not add multi-tenant auth.
34	
35	**Decided 2026-07-29.**
36	
37	Each operator runs their own container with their own `FOSSA_API_TOKEN`. One token per process,
38	supplied via environment at run time.
39	
40	This is a **product constraint, not a technical limitation.** Multi-tenant FOSSA hosting is FOSSA,
41	Inc.'s own business and we are deliberately not building toward competing with it.
42	
43	**Consequences:**
44	
45	- `FOSSA_API_TOKEN` from the environment is the correct and complete auth model. Do not add
46	  `token_verifier`, OAuth, or per-request credential plumbing.
47	- `stdio` is the default transport and the intended deployment shape.
48	- `streamable-http` remains available but binds `127.0.0.1` by default. Keep that default.
49	  **Kubernetes is the one sanctioned exception:** a pod must bind `0.0.0.0` or the Service can never
50	  reach it, so `lab-fleet/09-mcp/fossa-mcp.yaml` sets `FOSSA_HTTP_HOST=0.0.0.0`.
51	- **The sdf1 deployment is reachable at `https://fossa-mcp.ash4d.com/mcp`** (Traefik Ingress,
52	  cert-manager `letsencrypt-dns`). This is a LAN-scoped exposure, not a public one: the Cloudflare
53	  record is public but points at the private Traefik address `192.168.7.150`, so it resolves
54	  everywhere and connects only from inside the network. Only `/mcp` is routed; `/healthz` stays
55	  cluster-internal.
56	
57	  The boundary that makes this acceptable is the private target address, nothing else — the server
58	  still authenticates no callers, so anyone who reaches that host gets the token's full read access.
59	  A Cloudflare Tunnel, a public A record, or a LoadBalancer on a routable address all cross that
60	  boundary and require an authenticating middleware in front first.
61	- `FossaClient` is a single lifespan-scoped instance with one connection pool. Correct *because* of
62	  this decision; it would be wrong under multi-tenancy.
63	- **The server executes every request with the single token it was started with.** Exposing the HTTP
64	  transport to multiple users grants them all of that token's access. This must stay documented in
65	  the README.
66	
67	---
68	
69	## 3. Apache-2.0, not MIT.
70	
71	**Decided 2026-07-29.**
72	
73	The full runtime dependency tree (36 packages at `mcp` 1.28.1) is permissive — MIT, BSD-2/3-Clause,
74	Apache-2.0, ISC, MIT-0, PSF-2.0 — with no GPL, LGPL, or AGPL. Every inbound license is compatible
75	with any permissive outbound license, so compatibility did not constrain the choice; it was made on
76	merit for distribution to businesses:
77	
78	- **Explicit patent grant (§3)**, which MIT lacks. Enterprise legal review routinely flags that gap.
79	- **Explicit trademark disclaimer (§6)**, which matters here — see below.
80	- **NOTICE mechanism (§4)** carries the unofficial-tool disclaimer through redistribution.
81	
82	**Obligations to keep meeting:**
83	
84	- `certifi` is **MPL-2.0** — weak, file-level copyleft. It constrains nothing in our code (we do not
85	  modify it), but container images redistribute its binary, so its license text must ship in the
86	  image. Ship a consolidated third-party license file at a documented path.
87	- SUSE BCI base images carry SUSE's own terms, independent of our Apache-2.0 grant. Do not conflate
88	  them in documentation.
89	
90	---
91	
92	## 4. This is an unofficial tool. Keep saying so.
93	
94	**Decided 2026-07-29.**
95	
96	"FOSSA" is a trademark of FOSSA, Inc., used here nominatively to identify the API this software
97	talks to. The project is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or supported by FOSSA, Inc.
98	
99	The disclaimer must appear in `NOTICE`, the README, the OCI image description, and the Docker Hub
100	overview. Do not adopt FOSSA branding, and do not attribute authorship to FOSSA — an earlier draft
101	of `pyproject.toml` listed `support@fossa.com` as the package author, which was incorrect and is
102	exactly the failure mode to avoid.
103	
104	---
105	
106	## 5. The server is no longer wholly read-only. Security policy writes are permitted.
107	
108	**Decided 2026-07-31. This reverses part of decision-adjacent scope set on 2026-07-29.**
109	
110	`FOSSA_MCP_IMPLEMENTATION_SCOPE.md` §3.3 lists "policy modification" as out of scope, and the README
111	promised "this version is read-only and does not modify FOSSA state." Both were accurate and both
112	are now partly obsolete: the server can assign a FOSSA security policy to a project and turn on the
113	enforcement that blocks packages violating it.
114	
115	This was an explicit, informed product call — the read-only guarantee was named as the cost and
116	accepted. The scope document is a frozen requirements artifact and is deliberately **not** edited to
117	match; this entry is the record that the two now disagree, and this entry wins.
118	
119	**What is writable, and nothing else:**
120	
121	| Tool | Endpoint | Effect |
122	|------|----------|--------|
123	| `fossa_enable_security_policy` | `PUT /projects/{locator}` | Sets `securityPolicyId`, `securityIssueScanningEnabled`, `securityStatusCheckEnabled` |
124	| `fossa_assign_security_policy_to_projects` | `PUT /v2/projects/policy` | Assigns one policy id to explicitly named projects |
125	
126	Everything else in §3.3 stays out of scope. Issue ignoring, project deletion, label modification,
127	license conclusions, and disputes remain unimplemented.
128	
129	**Consequences:**
130	
131	- **`FOSSA_ALLOW_WRITES` defaults to false and must stay that way.** Both write tools refuse before
132	  issuing any request when it is off. A server that is merely *capable* of writing is not the same
133	  risk as one that will; under decision 2 every caller shares one token, so the default must be the
134	  safe one. `tests/test_mcp_integration.py` asserts a default-configured server refuses the write.
135	- The bulk endpoint's "apply to all projects matching these filters" mode is deliberately not
136	  exposed. `locators` is always an explicit list. A model that misreads a filter should not be able
137	  to re-policy an entire organization in one call.
138	- `FossaClient` retries writes. That is safe only because both endpoints are `PUT` and assign rather
139	  than accumulate. Adding `POST` or `PATCH` requires revisiting the retry loop first.
140	- `readOnlyHint` is now per-tool rather than blanket. The integration test partitions the tool list
141	  into declared read and write sets and fails if a tool's annotation disagrees with its set.
142	
143	**Why there is no "block this package" tool:** FOSSA has no per-package block primitive. A package is
144	blocked by an assigned security policy raising a vulnerability issue against it and the CI status
145	check then failing the build. `fossa_enable_security_policy` turns that combination on; that *is* the
146	block. Nor is there a create-policy or list-policies endpoint in the vendored spec, so policies are
147	authored in the FOSSA web app and addressed here by the numeric id in their URL.
148	
149	---
150	
151	## 6. The local policy overlay may only tighten, never loosen.
152	
153	**Decided 2026-07-31.**
154	
155	`FOSSA_POLICY_FILE` points at a JSON document of local security rules — CVSS ceilings, denied CVEs,
156	denied packages — evaluated by `fossa_evaluate_security_policy` on top of FOSSA's own findings.
157	
158	**An active FOSSA vulnerability finding always blocks, and no local rule can clear it.** Exceptions
159	in the overlay suppress blocks the *overlay itself* introduced and nothing more. The asymmetry is
160	the design: a file on the MCP server's disk must not be able to wave through a live finding from the
161	system of record, because the resulting verdict would look authoritative while being weaker than
162	what FOSSA says. `tests/test_policy.py` pins this.
163	
164	**Consequences:**
165	
166	- Exceptions require a `reason` and should carry an `expires` date. An expired exception stops
167	  applying and is reported on the verdict, so a package does not silently revert to blocked with no
168	  explanation.
169	- A configured-but-broken policy file raises rather than degrading to "no policy." A typo in a path
170	  must not quietly weaken the security posture.
171	- The file is JSON, not YAML. YAML reads better, but every runtime dependency is enumerated in
172	  `NOTICE` and the generated third-party license file per decision 3, and policy file ergonomics do
173	  not justify adding PyYAML to that tree.
174	- `projectDefaultStatusCheckFilterVulnerability` (FOSSA's status-check severity threshold) is
175	  reported verbatim and never interpreted. Its integer scale is undocumented in the vendored
176	  OpenAPI spec — do not invent a mapping for it.
177	
178	---
179	
180	## 7. Full API parity is the goal. Coverage is tiered, not ungated.
181	
182	**Decided 2026-07-31.** Requested directly; the driver was a FOSSA engineer asking for complete
183	write coverage during an interview.
184	
185	The target is all 271 documented operations — 157 `GET`, 114 write. `FOSSA_MCP_IMPLEMENTATION_SCOPE.md`
186	§3.3 forbids most of this. That document is a frozen requirements artifact and stays unedited; this
187	entry supersedes it, and `API_PARITY_PLAN.md` holds the domain inventory and running status.
188	
189	**Consequences:**
190	
191	- **Tool shape is a tiered hybrid, not 1:1.** Individual tools for domains an operator drives by
192	  hand; grouped `section`/`action` tools for configuration long tails. Organization Settings is 57
193	  operations of near-identical `get/patch/put` triples and becomes ~3 tools, not 57. Target is ~60
194	  tools for 271 operations — 271 tools would exceed what MCP clients handle, and selection accuracy
195	  degrades well before that limit.
196	- **Grouped tools still validate `section` against a `Literal`.** An unknown section must fail at
197	  the client as a schema error, not reach FOSSA as a 404. This is what keeps a grouped tool from
198	  degenerating into the generic `fossa_request` proxy that §3.3 rules out — that exclusion stands.
199	- **Three write tiers, none implying another** (`src/fossa_mcp/writes.py`): `WRITE`, `DESTRUCTIVE`
200	  (deletes and unbounded bulk targets), `ADMIN` (SAML, OIDC, roles, service accounts, team
201	  membership). Higher tiers require `FOSSA_ALLOW_WRITES` alongside their own flag, so a
202	  half-configured deployment fails closed.
203	- **Tier follows blast radius, not HTTP verb.** `PUT /v2/projects/policy` with `locators=all`
204	  re-policies an entire organization from one call, so it is `DESTRUCTIVE` despite being a `PUT`.
205	- **`POST` and `PATCH` are never retried** (`client.py`, `_IDEMPOTENT_METHODS`). A replayed create
206	  is a duplicate team or a duplicate service account. Do not make the retry loop uniform.
207	- **The ADMIN tier should stay off on the sdf1 deployment.** Under decision 2 the server
208	  authenticates no callers and shares one token; `https://fossa-mcp.ash4d.com/mcp` is reachable
209	  from anywhere on the LAN. Identity and access-control writes behind an unauthenticated endpoint
210	  are a materially different exposure from reading dependency lists, and the private target address
211	  is the only boundary in place.
212

- **The server executes every request with the single token it was started with.** Exposing the HTTP
  transport to multiple users grants them all of that token's access. This must stay documented in
  the README.

---

## 3. Apache-2.0, not MIT.

**Decided 2026-07-29.**

The full runtime dependency tree (36 packages at `mcp` 1.28.1) is permissive — MIT, BSD-2/3-Clause,
Apache-2.0, ISC, MIT-0, PSF-2.0 — with no GPL, LGPL, or AGPL. Every inbound license is compatible
with any permissive outbound license, so compatibility did not constrain the choice; it was made on
merit for distribution to businesses:

- **Explicit patent grant (§3)**, which MIT lacks. Enterprise legal review routinely flags that gap.
- **Explicit trademark disclaimer (§6)**, which matters here — see below.
- **NOTICE mechanism (§4)** carries the unofficial-tool disclaimer through redistribution.

**Obligations to keep meeting:**

- `certifi` is **MPL-2.0** — weak, file-level copyleft. It constrains nothing in our code (we do not
  modify it), but container images redistribute its binary, so its license text must ship in the
  image. Ship a consolidated third-party license file at a documented path.
- SUSE BCI base images carry SUSE's own terms, independent of our Apache-2.0 grant. Do not conflate
  them in documentation.

---

## 4. This is an unofficial tool. Keep saying so.

**Decided 2026-07-29.**

"FOSSA" is a trademark of FOSSA, Inc., used here nominatively to identify the API this software
talks to. The project is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or supported by FOSSA, Inc.

The disclaimer must appear in `NOTICE`, the README, the OCI image description, and the Docker Hub
overview. Do not adopt FOSSA branding, and do not attribute authorship to FOSSA — an earlier draft
of `pyproject.toml` listed `support@fossa.com` as the package author, which was incorrect and is
exactly the failure mode to avoid.

---

## 5. The server is no longer wholly read-only. Security policy writes are permitted.

**Decided 2026-07-31. This reverses part of decision-adjacent scope set on 2026-07-29.**

`FOSSA_MCP_IMPLEMENTATION_SCOPE.md` §3.3 lists "policy modification" as out of scope, and the README
promised "this version is read-only and does not modify FOSSA state." Both were accurate and both
are now partly obsolete: the server can assign a FOSSA security policy to a project and turn on the
enforcement that blocks packages violating it.

This was an explicit, informed product call — the read-only guarantee was named as the cost and
accepted. The scope document is a frozen requirements artifact and is deliberately **not** edited to
match; this entry is the record that the two now disagree, and this entry wins.

**What is writable, and nothing else:**

| Tool | Endpoint | Effect |
|------|----------|--------|
| `fossa_enable_security_policy` | `PUT /projects/{locator}` | Sets `securityPolicyId`, `securityIssueScanningEnabled`, `securityStatusCheckEnabled` |
| `fossa_assign_security_policy_to_projects` | `PUT /v2/projects/policy` | Assigns one policy id to explicitly named projects |

Everything else in §3.3 stays out of scope. Issue ignoring, project deletion, label modification,
license conclusions, and disputes remain unimplemented.

**Consequences:**

- **`FOSSA_ALLOW_WRITES` defaults to false and must stay that way.** Both write tools refuse before
  issuing any request when it is off. A server that is merely *capable* of writing is not the same
  risk as one that will; under decision 2 every caller shares one token, so the default must be the
  safe one. `tests/test_mcp_integration.py` asserts a default-configured server refuses the write.
- The bulk endpoint's "apply to all projects matching these filters" mode is deliberately not
  exposed. `locators` is always an explicit list. A model that misreads a filter should not be able
  to re-policy an entire organization in one call.
- `FossaClient` retries writes. That is safe only because both endpoints are `PUT` and assign rather
  than accumulate. Adding `POST` or `PATCH` requires revisiting the retry loop first.
- `readOnlyHint` is now per-tool rather than blanket. The integration test partitions the tool list
  into declared read and write sets and fails if a tool's annotation disagrees with its set.

**Why there is no "block this package" tool:** FOSSA has no per-package block primitive. A package is
blocked by an assigned security policy raising a vulnerability issue against it and the CI status
check then failing the build. `fossa_enable_security_policy` turns that combination on; that *is* the
block. Nor is there a create-policy or list-policies endpoint in the vendored spec, so policies are
authored in the FOSSA web app and addressed here by the numeric id in their URL.

---

## 6. The local policy overlay may only tighten, never loosen.

**Decided 2026-07-31.**

`FOSSA_POLICY_FILE` points at a JSON document of local security rules — CVSS ceilings, denied CVEs,
denied packages — evaluated by `fossa_evaluate_security_policy` on top of FOSSA's own findings.

**An active FOSSA vulnerability finding always blocks, and no local rule can clear it.** Exceptions
in the overlay suppress blocks the *overlay itself* introduced and nothing more. The asymmetry is
the design: a file on the MCP server's disk must not be able to wave through a live finding from the
system of record, because the resulting verdict would look authoritative while being weaker than
what FOSSA says. `tests/test_policy.py` pins this.

**Consequences:**

- Exceptions require a `reason` and should carry an `expires` date. An expired exception stops
  applying and is reported on the verdict, so a package does not silently revert to blocked with no
  explanation.
- A configured-but-broken policy file raises rather than degrading to "no policy." A typo in a path
  must not quietly weaken the security posture.
- The file is JSON, not YAML. YAML reads better, but every runtime dependency is enumerated in
  `NOTICE` and the generated third-party license file per decision 3, and policy file ergonomics do
  not justify adding PyYAML to that tree.
- `projectDefaultStatusCheckFilterVulnerability` (FOSSA's status-check severity threshold) is
  reported verbatim and never interpreted. Its integer scale is undocumented in the vendored
  OpenAPI spec — do not invent a mapping for it.

---

## 7. Full API parity is the goal. Coverage is tiered, not ungated.

**Decided 2026-07-31.** Requested directly; the driver was a FOSSA engineer asking for complete
write coverage during an interview.

The target is all 271 documented operations — 157 `GET`, 114 write. `FOSSA_MCP_IMPLEMENTATION_SCOPE.md`
§3.3 forbids most of this. That document is a frozen requirements artifact and stays unedited; this
entry supersedes it, and `API_PARITY_PLAN.md` holds the domain inventory and running status.

**Consequences:**

- **Tool shape is a tiered hybrid, not 1:1.** Individual tools for domains an operator drives by
  hand; grouped `section`/`action` tools for configuration long tails. Organization Settings is 57
  operations of near-identical `get/patch/put` triples and becomes ~3 tools, not 57. Target is ~60
  tools for 271 operations — 271 tools would exceed what MCP clients handle, and selection accuracy
  degrades well before that limit.
- **Grouped tools still validate `section` against a `Literal`.** An unknown section must fail at
  the client as a schema error, not reach FOSSA as a 404. This is what keeps a grouped tool from
  degenerating into the generic `fossa_request` proxy that §3.3 rules out — that exclusion stands.
- **Three write tiers, none implying another** (`src/fossa_mcp/writes.py`): `WRITE`, `DESTRUCTIVE`
  (deletes and unbounded bulk targets), `ADMIN` (SAML, OIDC, roles, service accounts, team
  membership). Higher tiers require `FOSSA_ALLOW_WRITES` alongside their own flag, so a
  half-configured deployment fails closed.
- **Tier follows blast radius, not HTTP verb.** `PUT /v2/projects/policy` with `locators=all`
  re-policies an entire organization from one call, so it is `DESTRUCTIVE` despite being a `PUT`.
- **`POST` and `PATCH` are never retried** (`client.py`, `_IDEMPOTENT_METHODS`). A replayed create
  is a duplicate team or a duplicate service account. Do not make the retry loop uniform.
- **The ADMIN tier should stay off on the sdf1 deployment.** Under decision 2 the server
  authenticates no callers and shares one token; `https://fossa-mcp.ash4d.com/mcp` is reachable
  from anywhere on the LAN. Identity and access-control writes behind an unauthenticated endpoint
  are a materially different exposure from reading dependency lists, and the private target address
  is the only boundary in place.

Both authorized items are done. Summary:

## What shipped on `block-package-tools`

Three commits, on the correct base — local `main` was stale, so the docs commit was cut from a `main` that predated PR #2 and had no `writes.py`. Rebased onto `origin/main` first.

**`fossa_block_package`** — `POST /packages/{locator}/rules`, tier `WRITE`, `idempotentHint=True`.
**`fossa_unblock_package`** — `GET /policies/{id}` then `PUT /policies/{id}/rules`, tier **`DESTRUCTIVE`**.

On the tier judgement call the handoff left open: destructive. It removes state *and* its blast radius is every rule on the policy rather than the one named, which is exactly the boundary decision 7 draws. It reads the policy immediately before the write, reports the surviving rule set in `data.rules_sent`, and short-circuits without writing when there's no matching rule.

Three input-model refusals, each preventing a bad write rather than a bad request:
- a versioned locator (`pip+aiofile$1.2.3`) is rejected — FOSSA carries version scope in the body, so sending it as identity creates a rule matching nothing;
- `versions=[]` is rejected *although FOSSA accepts it*, because FOSSA reads it as every version;
- a policy body without a recognizable `rules` array raises instead of PUTting an empty array, which would wipe the policy.

`client.py`'s `json_body` now accepts a list — the unblock body is a bare top-level array.

172 tests pass; ruff and pyright clean.

## Live validation — passed

Drove the real tool functions against Ash4d, so the tools are what got verified:

```
block          -> rule 58586851 blacklisted_dependency pip+aiofile, versionType ALL
block again    -> same ruleId, no duplicate          (idempotency confirmed)
unblock        -> removed 1, sent 4 surviving rules  (PUT under Bearer — the gap)
verify         -> rule set identical to baseline
unblock again  -> no-op path, nothing sent
```

The unblock `PUT` under Bearer auth was the one thing never proven — the prior session captured it from the browser. It works. Lab org is back at baseline.

## DECISIONS.md §5

Both false claims struck through rather than deleted, with a dated correction underneath. The struck text stays because the *general* lesson is the useful part: the vendored spec describes what FOSSA documents, not what FOSSA does. §5's writable table, the retry note (replayable `PUT`s vs. the never-replayed `POST`), and the destructive-tier rationale are current.

## Still queued

1. The summary you can paste into an email to Chelsea — tools now exist, so it's unblocked. I'd rather you frame it than have me guess at tone.
2. Push `block-package-tools` and open the PR (it's local-only right now).
3. Register the ~50 parity tools in `server.py` and push `api-parity`.

Two unrelated things I noticed and left alone: an untracked `skills/` at the repo root (five skills from the parallel session that were meant for `.claude/skills/`), and a stray `.venv 2` directory.

---
name: fossa-license-review
description: Run a customer-facing, obligation-oriented license audit of a FOSSA project — classify every license by what it actually obligates in this customer's distribution model and hand back an action list. Use when asked for a license audit, to review licensing issues, "can we ship this", any GPL/AGPL/copyleft question, license compliance for a release, or an M&A / due diligence licensing review.
---

# fossa-license-review

Read a project's licensing findings and full dependency list out of FOSSA,
establish how the customer actually distributes their software, classify every
license by the obligations it creates rather than by its name, and report which
findings require action for this customer and which are noise.

**Why this workflow exists:** FOSSA tools return license *names*. "GPL-3.0" is
not a verdict; it is an input to one. The same license is a shipping blocker in
a publicly distributed binary and a non-event in a SaaS backend, and a linter
with a copyleft license usually obligates nobody. The judgment that converts
names into obligations lives here, not in the API.

**The honest framing, stated up front and never dropped:** the obligation
classes below are settled, mainstream readings of these licenses, but the
distribution model and linkage facts they key off are *your assessment of the
customer's situation*, gathered in step 1. State that basis in the report. A
finding classified against a guessed distribution model is worse than an
unclassified one.

For a ranked score across a portfolio instead of a per-project obligations
audit, use [[fossa-suggest-score]] — same copyleft tiers, quantitative track.
This skill is the qualitative audit. Ask which project if it isn't named.
Everything else below is procedure.

## 1. Establish the distribution model first

Everything downstream depends on this, so ask — or infer from the repo,
deployment config, or what the user has already said — before pulling a single
finding. Four models, in descending order of how much they obligate:

1. **Publicly distributed** — binary, app store package, installer, npm/PyPI
   package, embedded firmware. Every distribution-triggered obligation is live.
2. **Distributed to customers** — on-prem installs, appliances, SDKs shipped
   under contract. Same obligations as public distribution; the audience is
   smaller but the trigger is identical.
3. **SaaS-only** — the code runs on the customer's servers and only its
   *output* reaches users. GPL, LGPL, and MPL obligations do **not** reach this
   deployment, because they trigger on distribution of the software itself.
   **AGPL is the exception that does reach SaaS — flag it loudly.** Its
   network-interaction clause is exactly the case the license was written for.
4. **Internal-only** — tooling, services, and scripts that never leave the
   organization. Almost nothing fires; attribution obligations technically
   attach to copies but there is no external audience.

Also establish, where knowable, **how copyleft dependencies are linked**:
static linking, dynamic linking, or a separate process. It decides LGPL
outcomes — statically linked LGPL in a distributed binary obligates you to
enable relinking (ship object files or use dynamic linking); dynamically linked
or process-separated LGPL asks only for attribution and the LGPL'd source.
When the repo is on disk, this is often a manifest or build-config read, not a
judgment call. When it is not knowable, pick the likelier default, say so, and
state what changes if it is wrong.

## 2. Pull the findings

######## fossa-api-audit
---
name: fossa-api-audit
description: Audit the FOSSA MCP server against its vendored OpenAPI spec and the live API - enumerate documented operations, map registered tools to them, live-verify every read endpoint, and prove the write gate refuses without a single HTTP call. Use when asked whether the endpoints are alive and accessible, whether the tool surface matches the documented API, for a coverage matrix or parity check, to look for spec drift, or after regenerating the spec or registering new tools.
---

# fossa-api-audit

Parse the vendored spec, derive the registered tool surface from the code as it
sits on disk, cross them into a coverage matrix, exercise every read endpoint
against the live API, run the refusal tests to prove the write gate holds, and
report the gaps.

**Why this workflow exists:** three surfaces drift independently. The vendored
spec (`spec/fossa-openapi.json`) is regenerated from FOSSA's published swagger
and grows on FOSSA's schedule; the registered tool list changes per branch —
this repo has had 9 tools on one branch and 13 on another *at the same time*,
with tool modules that exist but are not imported; and the live API answers for
what actually works today, for this org, with this token. An audit that
hardcodes any of the three answers a question nobody asked.

**The honest framing, stated up front and never dropped:** "live-verified"
means one successful call, from one org, at one moment. And the spec cannot
always be failed against: several GET operations declare a bodyless or
property-less 200 (6 of 157 at API 4.34.55, `GET /projects/{locator}` the
known worst case), so a live response full of fields the spec never mentions is
a **spec gap to report, not a server bug to flag**. Keep the two verdicts
separate everywhere they appear.

Run from the repo root. Results are branch-specific — name the branch
(`git branch --show-current`) in the report, first line.

## 1. Enumerate the documented surface

######## fossa-attribution
---
name: fossa-attribution
description: Produce a shippable third-party attribution document (NOTICE / THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES) for a FOSSA project from its attribution report. Use when asked for a NOTICE file, third-party licenses, an attribution report, open source notices, license texts for a release, or a list of a project's dependencies with their licenses and copyright holders.
---

# fossa-attribution

Pin a FOSSA project revision, pull its attribution report, agree the inclusion
scope with the user, and write the attribution file(s) — a NOTICE-style summary
and/or a full THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES with complete license texts — with every
unresolvable entry flagged rather than dropped.

**Why this workflow exists:** most licenses that permit redistribution require
notice in return — the license text, the copyright line, or both, preserved in
the shipped artifact. The failure mode is not producing an ugly file; it is
producing a *plausible-looking* file with silent gaps. A dependency missing
from the notices is a compliance hole nobody will spot by reading the file,
which is why steps 5 and 6 (flag the gaps, reconcile the counts) are the
non-negotiable part of this skill.

This skill produces the artifact. Whether attribution is required at all for a
given distribution, and which obligations attach, is the sibling skill
[[fossa-license-review]] — run that first when the question is "do we owe
notices" rather than "write the notices".

Ask which project if it isn't named. Everything else below is procedure.

## 1. Resolve the project and pin the revision

Never guess a locator, and never generate against "latest" without recording
what latest resolved to — an attribution document that cannot say which build
it covers is not evidence of anything.

######## fossa-spec-drift
---
name: fossa-spec-drift
description: Compare the vendored FOSSA OpenAPI spec against the live one and report which changes affect this repo's registered MCP tools. Use when asked what changed in the FOSSA API since the spec was vendored, whether the vendored spec is stale, whether an API change breaks or touches a registered tool, or before refreshing the counts in API_PARITY_PLAN.md.
---

# fossa-spec-drift

**To:** Chelsea Boling
**Subject:** Package blocking is built — and you were right about the quality policy

Chelsea,

Thanks again for the correction on where blocking actually lives. I went and built it, and I
want to give you the reasoning as well as the result, since the reasoning is the part that was
wrong in an interesting way.

---

## You were right, and I can now show it empirically

I had concluded from FOSSA's published OpenAPI spec that there was no per-package block
primitive — that a package gets blocked by an assigned *security* policy raising a vulnerability
issue plus the CI status check failing the build. I'd written that into the project's decision
log as settled.

It's wrong. A block is a `blacklisted_dependency` rule on a **quality** policy. I confirmed it
two ways beyond taking your word for it: the block dialog's policy selector offers only quality
policies — a security policy can't receive a block rule at all — and the rule that lands on the
policy after a block carries `type: "blacklisted_dependency"` with the versionless package
locator.

The error is worth naming precisely, because it wasn't a careless one: I generalized from the
*documented* surface to the product. The published spec has 271 operations and not one of them
touches policy rules — zero occurrences of `blockRule`, `blocklist`, or `denylist` anywhere in
it. So "not in the spec" quietly became "not in FOSSA." The decision log now says so, with the
original claim struck through rather than deleted, since the general lesson is the useful part.

## What the endpoints turned out to be

Before capturing anything, I wrote down what I expected the endpoint to look like and why,
ranked by confidence, and committed it. Then I captured the real traffic and scored the
prediction against it. That document is in the repo (`docs/ENDPOINT_INFERENCE.md`) if you want
to see the working rather than the answer.

The short version: I got the *shape* right and the *structure* wrong. I predicted an unversioned
path, a numeric policy id, and a versionless package locator — all correct. I predicted
block/unblock would be a symmetric verb pair on one resource, modeled on
`license-conclusions/conclude|unconclude`, which is the one documented operation of the same
kind. That was wrong, and no amount of reading the spec would have revealed it:

```
BLOCK    POST /api/packages/{locator}/rules    {"policyIds":[…], "versions":"ALL"|["3.11.1"]}
UNBLOCK  PUT  /api/policies/{policyId}/rules   [ …bare array of the surviving rule objects… ]
```

They aren't a pair at all. Block is package-scoped and additive. Unblock is policy-scoped and
replaces the policy's entire rule set — it's the policy editor's Save, not a delete of a named
rule. `DELETE /api/packages/{locator}/rules` is a 404.

## Three things I found that are probably yours, not mine

1. **CSRF protection on these write endpoints is session-only.** A cookie-authenticated POST
   from inside the app gets `403 "Missing or invalid authentication"` without the `_csrf` token.
   The same request with `Authorization: Bearer <API token>` and no CSRF header succeeds. That's
   conventional behavior and it's what makes a server-side tool possible at all — but it means
   the API token reaches undocumented write endpoints that the documented API doesn't expose. You
   may already intend that; I'd rather flag it than assume.

2. **Unblock is read-modify-write over the whole rule set with no precondition available.**
   There's no ETag, no `If-Match`, no version parameter. `rulesHash` comes back in the response
   but isn't accepted as a precondition. Two people removing different blocks from the same
   policy at the same time will silently clobber each other — last write wins and reinstates
   whatever the other removed. That's true of your own UI, not just of my tools.

3. **`GET /api/policies` exists and returns every policy with its full rule set** — id, type,
   title, `latestVersion`, and rules. It's not in the published spec either. It's genuinely
   useful; it means a caller doesn't have to read policy ids out of browser URLs, which is what
   my tools were doing before.

## What I built

Two tools, both gated off by default:

| Tool | Endpoint | Gate |
|------|----------|------|
| `fossa_block_package` | `POST /packages/{locator}/rules` | `FOSSA_ALLOW_WRITES` |
| `fossa_unblock_package` | `GET /policies/{id}` then `PUT /policies/{id}/rules` | `FOSSA_ALLOW_WRITES` **and** `FOSSA_ALLOW_DESTRUCTIVE` |

Unblock sits at the higher tier deliberately. It isn't just that it removes something — it's that
the only mechanism FOSSA offers rewrites every rule on the policy, so its blast radius is the
whole policy rather than the one rule named. It reads the policy immediately before writing and
reports the surviving rule set it's about to send, which is the most I can do about the
lost-update problem without a precondition to use.

Three input validations exist specifically to prevent a bad write rather than a bad request:

- A versioned locator (`pip+aiofile$1.2.3`) is rejected, because the version scope belongs in the
  body — sending it as part of the identity would create a rule matching nothing.
- `versions: []` is rejected **even though your API accepts it**, because your API reads it as
  every version. An accidentally-empty array shouldn't silently block a whole package; omitting
  the argument is the only way to say "all".
- A policy response without a recognizable `rules` array raises rather than sending an empty
  array, which would wipe the policy's rules.

172 tests pass, including contract tests pinning both request shapes and refusal tests asserting
zero HTTP calls when the gate is off. I also ran both tools against a live throwaway org
end to end: block creates the rule, re-blocking reuses the same `ruleId` rather than duplicating
(so it's genuinely idempotent), unblock removes only that rule and returns the policy to its
exact prior rule set, and a second unblock correctly does nothing.

Standing caveat, which is in the README at the point of use: these are endpoints FOSSA doesn't
document and owes no stability on. My tests pin my request shape; they can't detect FOSSA
changing its side.

## Five workflow skills, also now in the repo

Separately, I added five skills — procedures an assistant follows using the MCP tools, rather
than new tools. They're the part I'd actually want in front of a customer:

- **`fossa-license-review`** — an obligation-oriented license audit. It establishes the
  customer's distribution model first, then classifies findings by what they actually obligate.
  The same GPL-3.0 is a shipping blocker in a distributed binary and a non-event in a SaaS
  backend; AGPL is the exception that reaches SaaS. FOSSA returns license *names*, and a name
  isn't a verdict — this is the judgment layer on top.
- **`fossa-attribution`** — generates a shippable NOTICE / THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES from a pinned
  revision's attribution report. The design point is that it flags unresolvable entries and
  reconciles counts rather than producing a plausible-looking file with silent gaps.
- **`fossa-vuln-export`** — exports findings as OSV or CycloneDX 1.6 VDR, and diffs them against
  another scanner's output by normalizing both sides to (package identity, vulnerability
  identity). It states up front that such a diff measures detection differences, not correctness
  — a FOSSA-only finding isn't automatically a win.
- **`fossa-api-audit`** — cross-references the vendored spec, the registered tool surface, and
  the live API into a coverage matrix, and runs the refusal tests to prove the write gate holds.
  It keeps "spec gap" and "server bug" as separate verdicts, which matters because several
  documented GETs declare a property-less 200.
- **`fossa-spec-drift`** — operation-level diff of the vendored spec against the live one,
  reporting only the changes that land on a tool this server actually registers.

## Where it is

Repository: https://github.com/darthzen/fossa-mcp (Apache-2.0, and clearly labeled as unofficial
and unaffiliated — nominative use of the FOSSA name only, no branding).

The skills are on `main`. The block/unblock work is on the `block-package-tools` branch:
<PR LINK>

Happy to walk through any of it. The two things I'd most value your read on are whether the
Bearer-vs-CSRF asymmetry on those endpoints is intentional, and whether there's a supported way
to remove a single policy rule that I simply didn't find.

Rick

  — a FOSSA-only finding isn't automatically a win.
- **`fossa-api-audit`** — cross-references the vendored spec, the registered tool surface, and
  the live API into a coverage matrix, and runs the refusal tests to prove the write gate holds.
  It keeps "spec gap" and "server bug" as separate verdicts, which matters because several
  documented GETs declare a property-less 200.
- **`fossa-spec-drift`** — operation-level diff of the vendored spec against the live one,
  reporting only the changes that land on a tool this server actually registers.

## Where it is

Repository: https://github.com/darthzen/fossa-mcp (Apache-2.0, and clearly labeled as unofficial
and unaffiliated — nominative use of the FOSSA name only, no branding).

The skills are on `main`. The block/unblock work is on the `block-package-tools` branch:
<PR LINK>

Happy to walk through any of it. The two things I'd most value your read on are whether the
Bearer-vs-CSRF asymmetry on those endpoints is intentional, and whether there's a supported way
to remove a single policy rule that I simply didn't find.

Rick

1	# Calibration — worked examples
2	
3	Scored 2026-07-31 against the `darthzen` FOSSA org, 10 projects. Use these as
4	anchors so a finding scored today lands where a comparable one landed before.
5	All arithmetic shown; all FOSSA values are as returned by `fossa_project_posture`.
6	
7	**Transports and import surfaces below are verified from source**, not assumed —
8	see "The assumption that was wrong" at the end for why that distinction cost 12
9	points on one project and 12 on another, in opposite directions.
10	
11	## Result
12	
13	| Project | L/S/Q | Worst CVSS | Peak EPSS %ile | CIRS | Band |
14	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
15	| lab-memory | 0/5/0 | 8.7 | 92.6 | 93 | Critical |
16	| ollama-code-mcp | 0/6/0 | 8.7 | 92.6 | 81 | Critical |
17	| ollama-exporter | 0/5/0 | 7.5 | 84.6 | 56 | Medium |
18	| neuvector-mcp | 15/1/2 | 6.8 | 3.9 | 34 | Low |
19	| niffler | 16/1/19 | 6.1 | 10.7 | 31 | Low |
20	
21	Clean: dli-power-mcp, agent-build-tools, buzz-ash4d-com, fossa-mcp, lab-fleet.
22	
23	Verified deployment facts behind these numbers:
24	
25	| Project | Fact | Source |
26	|---|---|---|
27	| ollama-code-mcp | `DEFAULT_TRANSPORT = "stdio"` | `src/ollama_code_mcp/config.py:17` |
28	| lab-memory | `transport=os.environ.get("MCP_TRANSPORT", "streamable-http")`, k8s Ingress `mcp-memory.ash4d.com/mcp`, port 8765 | `mcp/src/lab_memory_mcp/server.py:79`, `mcp/k8s/ingress.yaml` |
29	| neuvector-mcp | `TRANSPORT` defaults `stdio`; http mode raises `ConfigError` without bearer tokens | `src/neuvector_mcp/server.py:127` |
30	| ollama-exporter | only `prometheus/prometheus/prompb` imported; explicit comment refusing `model/labels` | `internal/remotewrite/convert.go:19` |
31	| niffler | `postcss` appears only in `legacy/web/package-lock.json`; no user-CSS processing | repo grep |
32	
33	## Anchor 1 — reachable, high EPSS, local service
34	
35	**ollama-code-mcp / CVE-2025-53366 in `mcp 1.6.0`** (direct dep). Unhandled
36	exception on malformed requests. The parse path is shared across transports, so
37	stdio does not exempt it → Reachability 100. Local MCP server → Exposure 50.
38	Fix is 1.6.0 → 1.28.1, a minor bump → FixFriction 0.
39	
40	```
41	0.35×87.0 = 30.45      CVSS 8.7
42	0.25×92.6 = 23.15      EPSS 0.05981 → 92.563rd percentile
43	0.20×100  = 20.00      direct runtime dependency
44	0.15×50   =  7.50      local-only service
45	0.05×0    =  0.00      minor bump available
46	            ------
47	              81.1  →  81
48	```
49	
50	This is the calibration point for "genuinely urgent." Note EPSS did the work:
51	the same CVSS at the 28th percentile scores 65.
52	
53	## Anchor 2 — same package, transport-gated
54	
55	**ollama-code-mcp / CVE-2025-53365** — same package, same CVSS 8.7, but the
56	advisory scopes it to the streamable-HTTP transport. Verified stdio
57	(`config.py:17`) → Reachability 20, Exposure 20.
58	
59	```
60	0.35×87.0 = 30.45
61	0.25×28.0 =  7.00      EPSS 28.01st percentile
62	0.20×20   =  4.00      vulnerable transport not enabled
63	0.15×20   =  3.00
64	0.05×0    =  0.00
65	            ------
66	              44.45 →  44
67	```
68	
69	Identical CVSS, 37 points apart. Siblings under verified stdio:
70	CVE-2025-66416 → 44, CVE-2026-52869 → 38, CVE-2026-59950 → 35.
71	
72	## Anchor 2b — the same CVE, other side of the transport line
73	
74	**lab-memory / CVE-2025-53365** — byte-identical dependency (`mcp 1.6.0`), and it
75	runs streamable-HTTP behind a public k8s Ingress. Reachability 100, Exposure 100.
76	
77	```
78	0.35×87.0 = 30.45
79	0.25×28.0 =  7.00
80	0.20×100  = 20.00      transport in use
81	0.15×100  = 15.00      public ingress
82	0.05×0    =  0.00
83	            ------
84	              72.45 →  72
85	```
86	
87	**28 points on the same CVE and the same package version, decided entirely by a
88	one-line default in `server.py`.** Read the transport; never infer it from the
89	fact that something is "an MCP server."
90	
91	Siblings: CVE-2025-53366 → 89, CVE-2026-52869 → 66 (session hijack against a
92	*memory store* — the highest-consequence finding in the portfolio),
93	CVE-2025-66416 → 66 at Reachability 70 (Host-validation gap is present, but the
94	advisory's exploit scenario is localhost-specific), CVE-2026-59950 → 47
95	(WebSocket transport, not in use, even though the service is HTTP-exposed).
96	
97	Project: 89 + 1.5×3 = 93.5 → 93.
98	
99	## Anchor 3 — the CVSS disagreement
100	
101	**ollama-exporter / CVE-2019-3826 in `prometheus v0.51.2`** (direct dep). Stored
102	XSS in the Prometheus **web UI**. The project imports Prometheus as a Go library
103	and builds an exporter binary — the web UI is not compiled in.
104	
105	Naive scoring, treating a direct dep on a network-listening service as fully
106	reachable:
107	
108	```
109	0.35×61.0 = 21.35
110	0.25×84.6 = 21.15      EPSS 84.627th percentile
111	0.20×100  = 20.00
112	0.15×100  = 15.00
113	0.05×100  =  5.00      NO_SAFE_VERSION
114	            ------
115	              82.5  →  83   ← ranks #1 in the portfolio
116	```
117	
118	With reachability applied (component not in artifact → 20; not exposed → 20):
119	
120	```
121	21.35 + 21.15 + 4.00 + 3.00 + 5.00 = 54.5 → 55
122	```
123	
124	28 points, and the project drops from 1st to 3rd. Siblings: CVE-2026-42154
125	(remote-read endpoint, server-side) → 52, CVE-2026-42151 (azuread remote-write
126	config) → 40, CVE-2026-40179 → 30, CVE-2026-44903 (flag-gated legacy UI) → 27.
127	
128	Project roll-up: 55 + 1.5×1 (CVE-2026-42154 at 52 is the only other ≥50) = 56.5 → 56.
129	
130	## Anchor 4 — transitive, build-time only
131	
132	**niffler / CVE-2026-41305 in `postcss 8.4.31`** at depth 2. XSS requires the app
133	to parse user-submitted CSS and re-stringify it into a `<style>` tag; no such
134	path exists → Reachability 20. `postcss` appears only in
135	`legacy/web/package-lock.json` as a Next.js build-chain dependency — it never
136	runs in production → Exposure 20, not 100.
137	
138	```
139	0.35×61.0 = 21.35
140	0.25×10.7 =  2.67      EPSS 10.685th percentile
141	0.20×20   =  4.00
142	0.15×20   =  3.00      build-time only
143	0.05×0    =  0.00
144	            ------
145	              31.02 →  31
146	```
147	
148	"Internet-facing web app" describes the *project*; Exposure scores the
149	*dependency's* runtime. A build-chain package in a web app is build-time.
150	Scoring the project instead of the package cost 12 points here.
151	
152	## Anchor 5 — dev-only dependency
153	
154	**neuvector-mcp / CVE-2025-71176 in `pytest 8.4.2`** (direct, test-only). Local
155	tmpdir permissions. Fix requires 8.4.2 → 9.0.3, a major bump.
156	
157	```
158	0.35×68.0 = 23.80
159	0.25×3.9  =  0.97      EPSS 3.858th percentile
160	0.20×20   =  4.00      dev/test-only
161	0.15×20   =  3.00      build/test-time only
162	0.05×40   =  2.00      major bump
163	            ------
164	              33.77 →  34
165	```
166	
167	CVSS 6.8 landing at 34 is correct and is the point of the rubric.
168	
169	## Licensing anchors
170	
171	**niffler** — 16 flags: LGPL-3.0-or-later on `@img/sharp-*` prebuilt native
172	addons (dynamically loaded, not statically linked), MPL-2.0 on `next`, one
173	CC-BY-SA-4.0 policy conflict. Private repo, SaaS deployment.
174	
175	```
176	Copyleft 60 (weak: LGPL/MPL) × (Linkage 50 / 100) × 0.8 = 24
177	Distribution 20 (SaaS, private) × 0.2                   =  4
178	                                                          --
179	                                                          28
180	```
181	
182	**neuvector-mcp** — 15 flags: GPL-2.0-only discovered in `ruff` (direct dev
183	tool), GPL/LGPL/CPL in `Pygments` (transitive dev). Public repo, but neither
184	package is bundled into anything distributed.
185	
186	```
187	Copyleft 100 (strong GPL) × (Linkage 10 / 100) × 0.8 = 8
188	Distribution 100 (public) × 0.2                      = 20
189	                                                       --
190	                                                       28
191	```
192	
193	Both land at 28 by different routes — strong copyleft that ships nowhere, and
194	weak copyleft that ships dynamically. Neither project's score is set by
195	licensing: niffler takes 43 from postcss, neuvector-mcp takes 34 from pytest.
196	
197	An additive formula would have scored neuvector-mcp at 64 and made a linter the
198	org's third-biggest problem. This is why Linkage multiplies.
199	
200	## Remediation rollup
201	
202	18 vulnerability findings across the portfolio, four bumps:
203	
204	| Bump | Projects | Clears |
205	|---|---|---|
206	| `mcp` 1.6.0 → 1.28.1 | lab-memory, ollama-code-mcp | 10 — both Critical scores |
207	| `prometheus` v0.51.2 → v0.311.3 | ollama-exporter | 3 of 5; two are `NO_SAFE_VERSION` and all five unreachable |
208	| `pytest` → 9.0.3 | ollama-code-mcp, neuvector-mcp | 2 |
209	| `postcss` → 8.5.10 (npm override) | niffler | 1 |
210	
211	Recommended first: `mcp`. One dependency, two projects, retires the 93 and the 81.
212	
213	## The assumption that was wrong
214	
215	The first pass at this portfolio (same day, before the repos were read) assumed
216	stdio for all MCP servers and scored the *project's* exposure rather than the
217	*dependency's*. Both assumptions were stated in the report with deltas, which is
218	the only reason they were cheap to correct. Net effect once verified:
219	
220	| Project | Assumed | Verified | Why |
221	|---|---|---|---|
222	| lab-memory | 81 | **93** | defaults to streamable-http behind a public Ingress, not stdio |
223	| niffler | 43 | **31** | postcss is build-chain, not runtime |
224	| ollama-code-mcp | 81 | 81 | stdio assumption happened to be right |
225	| ollama-exporter | 56 | 56 | import-surface reasoning confirmed by grep |
226	
227	The ranking's top two swapped. **Read the transport and the import surface
228	before scoring whenever the repo is reachable** — it is a handful of greps and
229	it is the difference between a defensible number and a plausible one.
230

exception on malformed requests. The parse path is shared across transports, so
stdio does not exempt it → Reachability 100. Local MCP server → Exposure 50.
Fix is 1.6.0 → 1.28.1, a minor bump → FixFriction 0.

```
0.35×87.0 = 30.45      CVSS 8.7
0.25×92.6 = 23.15      EPSS 0.05981 → 92.563rd percentile
0.20×100  = 20.00      direct runtime dependency
0.15×50   =  7.50      local-only service
0.05×0    =  0.00      minor bump available
            ------
              81.1  →  81
```

This is the calibration point for "genuinely urgent." Note EPSS did the work:
the same CVSS at the 28th percentile scores 65.

## Anchor 2 — same package, transport-gated

**ollama-code-mcp / CVE-2025-53365** — same package, same CVSS 8.7, but the
advisory scopes it to the streamable-HTTP transport. Verified stdio
(`config.py:17`) → Reachability 20, Exposure 20.

```
0.35×87.0 = 30.45
0.25×28.0 =  7.00      EPSS 28.01st percentile
0.20×20   =  4.00      vulnerable transport not enabled
0.15×20   =  3.00
0.05×0    =  0.00
            ------
              44.45 →  44
```

Identical CVSS, 37 points apart. Siblings under verified stdio:
CVE-2025-66416 → 44, CVE-2026-52869 → 38, CVE-2026-59950 → 35.

## Anchor 2b — the same CVE, other side of the transport line

**lab-memory / CVE-2025-53365** — byte-identical dependency (`mcp 1.6.0`), and it
runs streamable-HTTP behind a public k8s Ingress. Reachability 100, Exposure 100.

```
0.35×87.0 = 30.45
0.25×28.0 =  7.00
0.20×100  = 20.00      transport in use
0.15×100  = 15.00      public ingress
0.05×0    =  0.00
            ------
              72.45 →  72
```

**28 points on the same CVE and the same package version, decided entirely by a
one-line default in `server.py`.** Read the transport; never infer it from the
fact that something is "an MCP server."

Siblings: CVE-2025-53366 → 89, CVE-2026-52869 → 66 (session hijack against a
*memory store* — the highest-consequence finding in the portfolio),
CVE-2025-66416 → 66 at Reachability 70 (Host-validation gap is present, but the
advisory's exploit scenario is localhost-specific), CVE-2026-59950 → 47
(WebSocket transport, not in use, even though the service is HTTP-exposed).

Project: 89 + 1.5×3 = 93.5 → 93.

## Anchor 3 — the CVSS disagreement

**ollama-exporter / CVE-2019-3826 in `prometheus v0.51.2`** (direct dep). Stored
XSS in the Prometheus **web UI**. The project imports Prometheus as a Go library
and builds an exporter binary — the web UI is not compiled in.

Naive scoring, treating a direct dep on a network-listening service as fully
reachable:

```
0.35×61.0 = 21.35
0.25×84.6 = 21.15      EPSS 84.627th percentile
0.20×100  = 20.00
0.15×100  = 15.00
0.05×100  =  5.00      NO_SAFE_VERSION
            ------
              82.5  →  83   ← ranks #1 in the portfolio
```

With reachability applied (component not in artifact → 20; not exposed → 20):

```
21.35 + 21.15 + 4.00 + 3.00 + 5.00 = 54.5 → 55
```

28 points, and the project drops from 1st to 3rd. Siblings: CVE-2026-42154
(remote-read endpoint, server-side) → 52, CVE-2026-42151 (azuread remote-write
config) → 40, CVE-2026-40179 → 30, CVE-2026-44903 (flag-gated legacy UI) → 27.

Project roll-up: 55 + 1.5×1 (CVE-2026-42154 at 52 is the only other ≥50) = 56.5 → 56.

## Anchor 4 — transitive, build-time only

**niffler / CVE-2026-41305 in `postcss 8.4.31`** at depth 2. XSS requires the app
to parse user-submitted CSS and re-stringify it into a `<style>` tag; no such
path exists → Reachability 20. `postcss` appears only in
`legacy/web/package-lock.json` as a Next.js build-chain dependency — it never
runs in production → Exposure 20, not 100.

```
0.35×61.0 = 21.35
0.25×10.7 =  2.67      EPSS 10.685th percentile
0.20×20   =  4.00
0.15×20   =  3.00      build-time only
0.05×0    =  0.00
            ------
              31.02 →  31
```

"Internet-facing web app" describes the *project*; Exposure scores the
*dependency's* runtime. A build-chain package in a web app is build-time.
Scoring the project instead of the package cost 12 points here.

## Anchor 5 — dev-only dependency

**neuvector-mcp / CVE-2025-71176 in `pytest 8.4.2`** (direct, test-only). Local
tmpdir permissions. Fix requires 8.4.2 → 9.0.3, a major bump.

```
0.35×68.0 = 23.80
0.25×3.9  =  0.97      EPSS 3.858th percentile
0.20×20   =  4.00      dev/test-only
0.15×20   =  3.00      build/test-time only
0.05×40   =  2.00      major bump
            ------
              33.77 →  34
```

CVSS 6.8 landing at 34 is correct and is the point of the rubric.

## Licensing anchors

**niffler** — 16 flags: LGPL-3.0-or-later on `@img/sharp-*` prebuilt native
addons (dynamically loaded, not statically linked), MPL-2.0 on `next`, one
CC-BY-SA-4.0 policy conflict. Private repo, SaaS deployment.

```
Copyleft 60 (weak: LGPL/MPL) × (Linkage 50 / 100) × 0.8 = 24
Distribution 20 (SaaS, private) × 0.2                   =  4
                                                          --
                                                          28
```

**neuvector-mcp** — 15 flags: GPL-2.0-only discovered in `ruff` (direct dev
tool), GPL/LGPL/CPL in `Pygments` (transitive dev). Public repo, but neither
package is bundled into anything distributed.

```
Copyleft 100 (strong GPL) × (Linkage 10 / 100) × 0.8 = 8
Distribution 100 (public) × 0.2                      = 20
                                                       --
                                                       28
```

Both land at 28 by different routes — strong copyleft that ships nowhere, and
weak copyleft that ships dynamically. Neither project's score is set by
licensing: niffler takes 43 from postcss, neuvector-mcp takes 34 from pytest.

An additive formula would have scored neuvector-mcp at 64 and made a linter the
org's third-biggest problem. This is why Linkage multiplies.

## Remediation rollup

18 vulnerability findings across the portfolio, four bumps:

| Bump | Projects | Clears |
|---|---|---|
| `mcp` 1.6.0 → 1.28.1 | lab-memory, ollama-code-mcp | 10 — both Critical scores |
| `prometheus` v0.51.2 → v0.311.3 | ollama-exporter | 3 of 5; two are `NO_SAFE_VERSION` and all five unreachable |
| `pytest` → 9.0.3 | ollama-code-mcp, neuvector-mcp | 2 |
| `postcss` → 8.5.10 (npm override) | niffler | 1 |

Recommended first: `mcp`. One dependency, two projects, retires the 93 and the 81.

## The assumption that was wrong

The first pass at this portfolio (same day, before the repos were read) assumed
stdio for all MCP servers and scored the *project's* exposure rather than the
*dependency's*. Both assumptions were stated in the report with deltas, which is
the only reason they were cheap to correct. Net effect once verified:

| Project | Assumed | Verified | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| lab-memory | 81 | **93** | defaults to streamable-http behind a public Ingress, not stdio |
| niffler | 43 | **31** | postcss is build-chain, not runtime |
| ollama-code-mcp | 81 | 81 | stdio assumption happened to be right |
| ollama-exporter | 56 | 56 | import-surface reasoning confirmed by grep |

The ranking's top two swapped. **Read the transport and the import surface
before scoring whenever the repo is reachable** — it is a handful of greps and
it is the difference between a defensible number and a plausible one.

1	---
2	name: fossa-suggest-score
3	description: Rank FOSSA projects by remediation urgency using a custom impact risk score that adds reachability and exposure to CVSS and EPSS. Use when asked which projects need remediation, how to prioritize FOSSA findings, to build or suggest a custom risk/impact score, to triage a FOSSA portfolio, or whenever FOSSA severity is being questioned as a prioritization signal.
4	---
5	
6	# fossa-suggest-score
7	
8	Read a FOSSA org's open issues, score every finding on a rubric that CVSS alone
9	cannot express, roll the findings up per project, and hand back a ranked
10	remediation list plus the version bumps that actually clear it.
11	
12	**Why this workflow exists:** CVSS ranks the *vulnerability*. It does not know
13	whether the vulnerable code path is compiled into your binary, whether the
14	service listens on a network, or whether the package is a test-only dependency.
15	In a real portfolio those three facts move findings by 25–30 points and reorder
16	the list. The score below is CVSS and EPSS — both straight out of FOSSA — plus
17	three judgment terms that you must gather and must label as judgment.
18	
19	**The honest framing, stated up front and never dropped:** the reachability and
20	exposure terms are *your assessment*, not FOSSA data. They carry 35% of the
21	weight between them. Every report states the assumption explicitly, and states
22	what the ranking becomes if the assumption is wrong. A score presented as if it
23	came out of FOSSA is worse than no score.
24	
25	Ask which org or project set if it isn't obvious. Everything else is procedure.
26	
27	## 1. Inventory
28	
29	```
30	fossa_list_projects(count=50, sort="issues-total_desc")
31	```
32	
33	That one call gives you titles, locators, `latestRevision.locator`, per-category
34	issue counts, and `public`. Projects with `issues.total == 0` need no
35	remediation — name them as clean and drop them; do not spend calls on them.
36	
37	Never guess a locator from a repo name. If the user named projects informally,
38	resolve each with `fossa_list_projects(title=...)` first.
39	
40	## 2. Pull posture for every project that has issues
41	
42	```
43	fossa_project_posture(project_locator=..., revision_locator=..., top_issue_count=15)
44	```
45	
46	**Issue these in parallel — one message, one call per project.** They are
47	independent and the round-trips dominate the runtime.
48	
49	`project_posture` is the right tool here: one call returns the CVE detail, CVSS,
50	**EPSS score and percentile**, `remediation` distances, dependency depth, and the
51	direct-dependencies-with-issues rollup. Reaching for `fossa_list_issues` per
52	category instead costs 3× the calls for less data.
53	
54	`top_issue_count=15` is enough for the vulnerability list in most projects. If a
55	project has more licensing issues than that, you do not need them all —
56	licensing scores cluster tightly by license family (step 5), so a sample plus
57	the category count is sufficient.
58	
59	**Project scope on `fossa_list_issues` requires `revision_locator` as well as
60	`project_locator`**, or the call fails validation. Only reach for it when you
61	need issues `project_posture` truncated away.
62	
63	## 3. Establish reachability and exposure
64	
65	Do this **before** scoring. This is the step that earns the skill its keep, and
66	it is not answerable from the CVE text.
67	
68	For each vulnerable package, answer three questions:
69	
70	1. **Is the vulnerable code path in the shipped artifact?** A Go binary that
71	   imports `prometheus` as a metrics library does not compile in the Prometheus
72	   web UI, the `/api/v1/read` endpoint, or the remote-write config — so the
73	   CVEs in those components are unreachable no matter how high the CVSS. Read
74	   the advisory for *which component* is affected, then check whether this
75	   project uses it.
76	2. **Is it a runtime or a dev/test dependency?** `pytest`, `ruff`, linters,
77	   build tooling — these never reach production and never reach a customer.
78	   They score low and they should.
79	3. **What transport / deployment does this thing actually run in?** An MCP
80	   server over stdio is untouched by CVEs in SSE, WebSocket, and streamable-HTTP
81	   transports. An MCP server over HTTP is fully exposed to all of them. Same
82	   package, same version, ~25 points apart.
83	
84	Where the answer is knowable, know it: read the repo's manifest, entry point, or
85	deployment config. Where it is not — transport is the usual one — **pick the
86	likelier default, score with it, and surface it as the named assumption with the
87	delta.** Do not silently assume, and do not refuse to score.
88	
89	Group findings by **package**, not by CVE, while you do this. Five CVEs in one
90	dependency is one version bump and one reachability judgment.
91	
92	## 4. Score each vulnerability finding
93	
94	```
95	CIRS = 0.35·Severity + 0.25·Exploit + 0.20·Reachability + 0.15·Exposure + 0.05·FixFriction
96	```
97	
98	Every term is 0–100. The result is 0–100.
99	
100	| Term | Source | Scale |
101	|---|---|---|
102	| **Severity** | FOSSA `cvss` × 10 | 0–100 |
103	| **Exploit** | FOSSA `epss.percentile` × 100 | 0–100 |
104	| **Reachability** | judgment, step 3 | 100 direct runtime dep · 70 transitive runtime · 20 dev/test-only **or** vulnerable component not in the shipped artifact |
105	| **Exposure** | judgment, step 3 | 100 network-listening service · 50 local-only service · 20 build/test-time only |
106	| **FixFriction** | FOSSA `remediation` | 0 minor bump · 40 major bump · 100 `NO_SAFE_VERSION` |
107	
108	Use **`epss.percentile`, not `epss.score`.** The raw score is a tiny probability
109	(0.00205) that contributes nothing on a 0–100 scale; the percentile is the
110	comparative signal you actually want, and the gap between them is large — 0.0598
111	raw is the 92.6th percentile.
112	
113	FixFriction is deliberately the smallest weight. It does not make a finding more
114	dangerous; it makes the finding more likely to sit unfixed, which is a real but
115	second-order concern. Never let it dominate.
116	
117	## 5. Score licensing on its own track
118	
119	Licensing findings are not vulnerabilities and the vulnerability formula
120	mis-scores them. Run them separately:
121	
122	```
123	LIS = Copyleft × (Linkage / 100) × 0.8 + Distribution × 0.2
124	```
125	
126	| Term | Scale |
127	|---|---|
128	| **Copyleft** | 100 strong (GPL, AGPL) · 60 weak (LGPL, MPL) · 20 permissive-with-notice |
129	| **Linkage** | 100 distributed and statically linked · 50 distributed, dynamically linked or separate process · 10 dev/build-only, never distributed |
130	| **Distribution** | 100 publicly distributed software · 50 distributed to customers · 20 internal or SaaS-only |
131	
132	Linkage **multiplies** rather than adds, on purpose. A GPL-2.0 discovered
133	license in a linter that ships to nobody is not a 100-point problem, and an
134	additive formula makes it one.
135	
136	Note what does and does not trigger an obligation: LGPL and MPL do not reach a
137	SaaS deployment, and dynamically-loaded native addons are not static linking.
138	AGPL is the exception that does reach SaaS — flag it loudly if you see it.
139	
140	**Project score = max(highest vulnerability CIRS, highest licensing LIS).** Quality
141	findings (outdated deps, native-code risk) do not score; report them as context.
142	
143	## 6. Roll up to the project
144	
145	```
146	Project CIRS = highest issue score + min(10, 1.5 × count of other issues scoring ≥ 50)
147	```
148	
149	The cap matters. Without it, a project with sixteen near-identical LGPL flags
150	outranks one with a 92nd-percentile RCE, and that is exactly the failure this
151	skill exists to prevent. Volume is a tiebreaker, never the driver.
152	
153	| Band | Score |
154	|---|---|
155	| Critical | ≥ 75 |
156	| High | 60–74 |
157	| Medium | 40–59 |
158	| Low | 20–39 |
159	| Informational | < 20 |
160	
161	Two projects that depend on the same package at the same version **should tie**.
162	Do not manufacture a difference to break it — say they tie and why, then break
163	it on deployment exposure if you actually know it differs.
164	
165	## 7. Report
166	
167	Lead with the ranked table: project, FOSSA issue counts as L/S/Q, worst raw
168	CVSS, peak EPSS percentile, and the CIRS with its band. Showing the raw inputs
169	next to the score is what lets the user check your judgment rather than take it.
170	
171	Then, in order:
172	
173	- **The formula and both rubric tables**, with each term marked FOSSA or
174	  judgment. The user asked for a *suggested* score; they cannot adopt or amend
175	  one they cannot see.
176	- **The assumptions**, called out as their own block, each with its delta:
177	  "scored as stdio; if any runs over HTTP these four CVEs go from ~40 to ~65 and
178	  the project moves to 91."
179	- **Per-project detail**, a short paragraph each, leading with whatever the score
180	  turned on.
181	- **The remediation table, grouped by package.** This is the payoff and it goes
182	  last because it is what the user acts on: bump, projects affected, issues
183	  cleared. Close by naming which single bump to do first and why.
184	
185	**Say when the score disagrees with CVSS, and say it as a finding.** "Raw CVSS
186	ranks this first at 83; reachability drops it to 56 because four of five CVEs
187	are in components an exporter binary does not compile in" is the most valuable
188	sentence in the report. Burying it wastes the whole exercise.
189	
190	## Traps
191	
192	- **`customRiskScore` is `null` on every issue until someone configures it.**
193	  Check it — if FOSSA already has custom scores, the user wants those reconciled
194	  with your suggestion, not overwritten by it. If it is null everywhere, say so:
195	  it tells them nothing custom is configured today.
196	- **Do not present judgment terms as FOSSA output.** Reachability and exposure
197	  are 35% of the weight and neither exists in the API.
198	- **Exposure scores the dependency's runtime, not the project's.** A build-chain
199	  package inside an internet-facing web app is build-time (20), not
200	  network-listening (100). Getting this backwards inflated a finding by 12 points
201	  on 2026-07-31.
202	- **Read the transport before scoring it.** Two MCP servers on the identical
203	  package version scored 28 points apart on the same CVE, decided by a one-line
204	  default. When the repo is on disk this is a grep, not a judgment call.
205	- **Do not skip clean projects silently.** "Five of ten have issues; the other
206	  five are clean" is information.
207	- **Weight sums to 1.0.** If you tune the weights for a user's environment —
208	  reasonable, and they may ask — re-normalize, and restate the changed formula in
209	  the report rather than quietly scoring against a different rubric than the one
210	  you printed.
211	
212	## Scope
213	
214	This skill reads FOSSA and produces an assessment. It does **not** write to
215	FOSSA, and it does **not** change the target repositories. When the fix is a
216	version bump — it nearly always is — recommend it and let the user decide; raise
217	it as its own task rather than editing their code here.
218	
219	Worked examples with full arithmetic, for calibrating new scores against past
220	ones: `references/calibration.md`.

mis-scores them. Run them separately:

```
LIS = Copyleft × (Linkage / 100) × 0.8 + Distribution × 0.2
```

| Term | Scale |
|---|---|
| **Copyleft** | 100 strong (GPL, AGPL) · 60 weak (LGPL, MPL) · 20 permissive-with-notice |
| **Linkage** | 100 distributed and statically linked · 50 distributed, dynamically linked or separate process · 10 dev/build-only, never distributed |
| **Distribution** | 100 publicly distributed software · 50 distributed to customers · 20 internal or SaaS-only |

Linkage **multiplies** rather than adds, on purpose. A GPL-2.0 discovered
license in a linter that ships to nobody is not a 100-point problem, and an
additive formula makes it one.

Note what does and does not trigger an obligation: LGPL and MPL do not reach a
SaaS deployment, and dynamically-loaded native addons are not static linking.
AGPL is the exception that does reach SaaS — flag it loudly if you see it.

**Project score = max(highest vulnerability CIRS, highest licensing LIS).** Quality
findings (outdated deps, native-code risk) do not score; report them as context.

## 6. Roll up to the project

```
Project CIRS = highest issue score + min(10, 1.5 × count of other issues scoring ≥ 50)
```

The cap matters. Without it, a project with sixteen near-identical LGPL flags
outranks one with a 92nd-percentile RCE, and that is exactly the failure this
skill exists to prevent. Volume is a tiebreaker, never the driver.

| Band | Score |
|---|---|
| Critical | ≥ 75 |
| High | 60–74 |
| Medium | 40–59 |
| Low | 20–39 |
| Informational | < 20 |

Two projects that depend on the same package at the same version **should tie**.
Do not manufacture a difference to break it — say they tie and why, then break
it on deployment exposure if you actually know it differs.

## 7. Report

Lead with the ranked table: project, FOSSA issue counts as L/S/Q, worst raw
CVSS, peak EPSS percentile, and the CIRS with its band. Showing the raw inputs
next to the score is what lets the user check your judgment rather than take it.

Then, in order:

- **The formula and both rubric tables**, with each term marked FOSSA or
  judgment. The user asked for a *suggested* score; they cannot adopt or amend
  one they cannot see.
- **The assumptions**, called out as their own block, each with its delta:
  "scored as stdio; if any runs over HTTP these four CVEs go from ~40 to ~65 and
  the project moves to 91."
- **Per-project detail**, a short paragraph each, leading with whatever the score
  turned on.
- **The remediation table, grouped by package.** This is the payoff and it goes
  last because it is what the user acts on: bump, projects affected, issues
  cleared. Close by naming which single bump to do first and why.

**Say when the score disagrees with CVSS, and say it as a finding.** "Raw CVSS
ranks this first at 83; reachability drops it to 56 because four of five CVEs
are in components an exporter binary does not compile in" is the most valuable
sentence in the report. Burying it wastes the whole exercise.

## Traps

- **`customRiskScore` is `null` on every issue until someone configures it.**
  Check it — if FOSSA already has custom scores, the user wants those reconciled
  with your suggestion, not overwritten by it. If it is null everywhere, say so:
  it tells them nothing custom is configured today.
- **Do not present judgment terms as FOSSA output.** Reachability and exposure
  are 35% of the weight and neither exists in the API.
- **Exposure scores the dependency's runtime, not the project's.** A build-chain
  package inside an internet-facing web app is build-time (20), not
  network-listening (100). Getting this backwards inflated a finding by 12 points
  on 2026-07-31.
- **Read the transport before scoring it.** Two MCP servers on the identical
  package version scored 28 points apart on the same CVE, decided by a one-line
  default. When the repo is on disk this is a grep, not a judgment call.
- **Do not skip clean projects silently.** "Five of ten have issues; the other
  five are clean" is information.
- **Weight sums to 1.0.** If you tune the weights for a user's environment —
  reasonable, and they may ask — re-normalize, and restate the changed formula in
  the report rather than quietly scoring against a different rubric than the one
  you printed.

## Scope

This skill reads FOSSA and produces an assessment. It does **not** write to
FOSSA, and it does **not** change the target repositories. When the fix is a
version bump — it nearly always is — recommend it and let the user decide; raise
it as its own task rather than editing their code here.

Worked examples with full arithmetic, for calibrating new scores against past
ones: `references/calibration.md`.

---
name: fossa-protect
description: Turn a project's FOSSA vulnerability findings into NeuVector WAF sensors and push them to the cluster. Use when asked to mitigate, compensate for, or "protect against" CVEs found by FOSSA, to write WAF sensors/rules for a project's dependencies, or whenever FOSSA findings and NeuVector need to be connected. Also use when asked to review or roll back sensors created this way.
---

# fossa-protect

Read a project's vulnerabilities out of FOSSA, decide which are actually
mitigable by a regex WAF, write sensors for those, and bind them to the right
NeuVector groups in an alert-only mode.

**Why this workflow exists:** so the security team can mitigate **immediately
and unilaterally**, without waiting on the dev team. In practice — especially
with legacy code — the upgrade can take years or never happen at all:
maintainers leave, nobody knows where the source lives or what server it runs
on. The sensor is a real mitigation in its own right, not a placeholder for a
fix that is presumed imminent. Plan for it to be the operative control
**indefinitely**: write comments that survive team turnover, validate rather
than assume, and treat the Protect-mode warning as more important the longer a
binding will live, not less.

**The honest framing, stated up front and never dropped:** a NeuVector WAF
sensor is *regex matched against request context* — nothing more. Only
upgrading the vulnerable dependency closes the CVE, so every report this skill
produces names the version bump that actually fixes the finding — as the
parallel dev-side track, not as a reason to withhold or undersell the
mitigation. Honesty cuts both ways: never inflate what a rule catches
(step 3's classification), and never dismiss a validated sensor as "just a
stopgap".

Ask which project if it isn't named. Everything else below is procedure.

## 1. Pull the findings

Resolve the project first — never guess a locator:

- `fossa_list_projects(title=...)` → the locator (e.g. `git+github.com/org/repo`).
  If the project was not named, `sort="issues-security_desc"` puts the candidates
  worth asking about at the top; offer those rather than the whole inventory.
- `fossa_list_issues(category="vulnerability", scope_type="project",
  project_locator=..., revision_locator=...)` — **project scope requires
  `revision_locator` as well**, or the call fails validation. Take it from the
  project's `latestRevision.locator`.
- `fossa_get_issue(...)` for anything whose CVE detail you actually need

Group findings by **package**, not by CVE. Five CVEs in one dependency is one
version bump, and that reframing is usually the most useful thing you can tell
the user.

## 2. Establish what is actually deployed

Do this **before** triage, not after. Triage is not answerable in the abstract:
whether a CVE is reachable at all depends on how this deployment is configured,
and getting that backwards means writing a sensor for something that cannot fire.

Confirm the workloads are running and serving traffic:

- `nv_list_workloads` / `kubectl get pods -n <ns>`
- `nv_list_groups(name_prefix="nv.<service>")` — plain listing truncates and is
  alphabetical, so the group you want may simply not be on the page
- `nv_list_waf_groups(bound_only=true)` for what already has sensors

Then read the deployment's actual configuration — Deployment, Service, Ingress,
ConfigMap. You are looking for the facts that decide reachability and that the
rules will be written against:

- **Which transport / protocol is really enabled.** A CVE in a transport this
  deployment does not use is not mitigable, it is *not applicable*, and saying so
  is worth more than a rule.
- **Whether auth is configured**, and what the vulnerable default actually is.
